content: Crowder's name for grooves that divide each beat of a slow 4/4 into more than 10 equal notes. The 11-tuplet is the mildest one. Quintuplet and septuplet grooves are the usual tuplet grooves of the band.
parameters: 11, 13, 15, 17 or 19 notes per beat. Examples of the pulse: 33 BPM and 58 BPM
where: Against the Fall of Night; Threshold; other tunes of the 2021 album

content: The 11 notes are grouped as in the Bulgarian dances gankino horo and kopanitsa, and as in a well-known drumline warm-up (Crowder likes drum corps). Neely finds the grouping 3+3+3+2 less natural.
parameters: 2+2+3+2+2 = quick, quick, slow, quick, quick
where: Against the Fall of Night (title track)

content: The groups differ by less than 100 ms. Thus listeners smooth 2+2+3+2+2 into three almost equal beats (4+3+4). They hear and move to a fast 3/4, not to the slow 4/4. Neely jokes that everything 'evolves to three'.
parameters: 58 BPM pulse: felt quarter = 174 BPM, beat ratio 4:3:4. 33 BPM pulse with 6+6+7: felt 3/4 near 99 BPM, beats of 574, 574 and 670 ms (computed)
where: Against the Fall of Night; Threshold

content: The band counts off and sets the click in 4/4 on the slow pulse. The parts are written in an odd metre with the tuplet number on top, one bar for each beat, because tuplets with syncopation are hard to read.
parameters: One bar of 11/16 = one beat of the slow 4/4 = 5.5 eighth notes
where: Against the Fall of Night (title track)

content: In the bridge an accent on each third 11-tuplet makes a three-feel against the 11.
parameters: Accent on notes 1, 4, 7, 10 and so on. The accent pattern and the 11-cycle meet again after 33 notes = 3 beats (computed)
where: Against the Fall of Night (title track), bridge

item: Change of subdivision on one pulse (7 against 11)
content: The band changes the number of notes per beat and keeps the pulse. From 11 to 7 sounds like a slower tempo; back to 11 sounds like a faster tempo. In the odd-metre parts this is written as a 7:11 polyrhythm.
parameters: At 58 BPM: 11 per beat = 10.6 notes per second; 7 per beat = 6.8 notes per second (computed)
where: Against the Fall of Night (title track), breakdown

content: The beat is divided in 5 and the notes come on parts 1 and 4. The feel is between straight and triplet swing: 'almost triplets, but not'. Crowder likes this feel.
parameters: Long to short = 3:2 (60 percent). Compare: straight 50 percent; septuplet swing 57.1; triplet swing 66.7. Jazz swing ratios in general: 1:1 to 3:1
where: Sequence Start; The Dark (written in quintuplets)

content: The beat is divided in 7 as 4+3. Neely used septuplets to get near a 'drunken' backbeat in a dubstep setting.
parameters: Long to short = 4:3 (57.1 percent)

item: The stock 5/4 pattern that Ether avoids
content: The pattern that most pieces in 5/4 use, as in Take Five.
parameters: 3+3+2+2 eighth notes (dotted quarter, dotted quarter, quarter, quarter). This value was not confirmed in a source

item: Clave of long and short pulses
content: A groove is made from uneven pulses in a fixed order. The backbeat is on long pulses 2 and 4, so the long pulses sound like the beats of a 4/4 bar and the short pulse like a small extra beat.
parameters: Long = dotted quarter (3 eighths). Short = quarter (2 eighths). Ratio 3:2. Pattern long, long, long, long, short = 14 eighths

item: Pulse morph (new subdivision of uneven pulses)
content: Crowder's idea: each long pulse gets 5 notes and the short pulse gets 3. The two note speeds are not the same. The band stretched the notes so that the long and short pulses keep their exact lengths. The other choice (even notes, pulse lengths only nearly right) sounds more organic but does not fit a laptop with layers on top.
parameters: 23 notes per cycle (5+5+5+5+3). Note length 0.600 eighth in the long pulses and 0.667 eighth in the short pulse: 11 percent longer (computed)

content: Estimate from the database tempo of 183 BPM for the quarter note. The fast notes of the second half are at the limit of rhythm perception.
parameters: Estimate: eighth = 164 ms; long pulse = 492 ms (122 BPM); cycle = 2.30 s; quintuplet note = 98 ms; triplet note of the short pulse = 109 ms

content: Each fifth eighth-note triplet becomes the new beat: a quarter note tied to a quarter-note triplet equals the new quarter note. The way back uses three quintuplets of the slow tempo. A reviewer describes the same device: the piece switches between 5 beats of triplets and 3 beats of quintuplets.
parameters: 136 BPM to 82 BPM. New tempo = old tempo x 3/5. 5 beats x 3 notes = 3 beats x 5 notes = 15 notes. General formula: new tempo / old tempo = number of pivot notes in the new bar / number in the old bar

content: A drum feature goes from quintuplets to sextuplets to septuplets; the quintuplet licks are felt as 2+3 or 3+2. In 5/4 the drums play kick, snare, snare, so a 3/4 waltz feel goes across the bar. Also: a kick on all five beats ('five-on-the-floor'); a five-note pattern in triplets on the cymbal, phrased 2+3; off-beat triplets in the first groove.
parameters: 5, 6, 7 notes per beat at 82 BPM = 6.8, 8.2, 9.6 notes per second (computed). 3-beat cell against a 5-beat bar: the two meet after 15 beats (computed)

content: Balkan groupings are a constant source. Titles and metres come from dances.
parameters: Bird on the Wing: 9/8 as 2+3+2+2. Paydushko Horo: from a 5/8 dance (2+3). Electro: a passage in 5/16. A live song in 7/8 with a clap pattern for the audience. Gankino and kopanitsa: 11 as 2+2+3+2+2

content: Aksak ('limping'): fast metres made by cells of 2 and 3 in a fixed order.
The limbs are divided left side against right side, not hands against feet. The left hand and left foot loop an ostinato on hi-hat and stack for the full song. The right side improvises.
parameters: 2 layers in one player: ostinato (left) and free part (right). Models named: Mike Mangini, Virgil Donati

content: Estimate from the database tempo of 108 BPM and the quintuplet groove that a reviewer describes. Each beat is then one bar of 5/16.
parameters: Estimate: 5 notes per beat at 108 BPM = 111 ms per note = 540 sixteenths per minute

item: Notes per beat used in the catalogue
content: The number of equal notes in one beat changes from piece to piece and inside a piece.
parameters: 3 (shuffle, triplet feel), 4, 5 (quintuplets), 6, 7 (septuplets), 11, 19. Combined grid of triplets and quintuplets: 15
where: All releases (list compiled from the sources)

content: Metres and groupings that the sources name for the pieces.
parameters: 4/4 on a slow pulse (written as one bar of 11/16 for each beat); 5/4; 7/4 as 3+3+3+3+2 eighths; 9/8 as 2+3+2+2; 9 as 3+3+3; 7/8; 5/16; chorus of 4/4 + 4/4 + 2/4; phrase of 17 as 4+4+1+4+4
where: All releases (list compiled from the sources)
source: neely-44; neely-cool7; waterson-whalefall; natebrowne-odd; neely-eu22; bluesuns-atfon

item: Ratios used for changes of speed
content: Ratios between two pulses or two note rates in the pieces.
parameters: 3:2 (long pulse to short pulse, Cool 7). 5:3 (old tempo to new tempo, Whalefall: 136 to 82 BPM). 11:7 (note rate on one pulse, title track of 2024). 3:1 (felt beat to written pulse: 174 to 58 BPM; 99 to 33 BPM). 5 notes in 3 eighths and 3 notes in 2 eighths (Cool 7)
where: Albums 2021 and 2024 (list compiled from the sources)

content: The groove is Moroccan chaabi. It is written in 3/4 and felt as a fast 12/8. League wanted some sections to feel in three and other sections in four. The krakeb play the gnawa rhythm mserah.
parameters: A transcriber gives 6/8 at 120 BPM in A Dorian. League: at that tempo the music "is gliding along"

content: Lingus is in 5/4. Outlier is in 6/8. Flood has a drum solo in 7/8. Between Worlds has verses in 3/4 and a chorus in 5/4. The riff of Bent Nails came from the drummer with no drums and no click: the band could not find beat one or the metre.
parameters: Metres: 5/4, 6/8, 7/8, 3/4 with 5/4, 12/8. The machine gives 4 beats in a bar for 11 of 22 tracks, 3 beats for 4 tracks, 5 beats for 1 track, and no clear value for 6 tracks
where: We Like It Here; Tell Your Friends; Somni; groundUP
source: ht-lingus; ht-outlier; md-2016a; wiki-somni; notreble-league2014; songbpm-sp

item: Several drum kits: one drummer for each section
content: One drummer plays the verse and a different drummer plays the chorus. The change is on the first beat of the section. The effect is one drummer who changes the tuning of the kit.
parameters: 3 kits on Empire Central; 4 kits on Somni. On Culcha Vulcha 2 drummers play on each track

item: Simple drum parts in a large band
content: The grooves are mostly simple patterns of kick, snare, and hi-hat. Toms are for colour and for transitions. League at first wanted no toms. The drummers and percussionists choose parts that fit together as layers.
parameters: Somni: 4 drummers and 4 percussionists; the drummers call the parts minimal

item: Layers in different metres and tempos
content: Recurrent: 4 drummers trade with sections of the orchestra; each drummer has a different click, thus several metres run together. Chimera: the ensemble divides into 4 groups in different keys and tempos; at the end 4 drummers play in 4 different time signatures under one horn line.
parameters: 4 layers at one time. League: Chimera was the "hardest thing" on the record

content: Tarova: South Asian percussion (kanjira) with a go-go feel. Semente: Brazilian (repinique, caixa, surdo, triangle). Grown Folks: a New Orleans parade beat. Quarter Master: the French Quarter. Xavi: Moroccan chaabi and gnawa. Bigly Strictness: a Turkish rhythm at half speed ('Funky Arap') on daf, bendir, and darbuka. Even Us: 3 Turkish bendirs and riq.
parameters: 1 traditional groove for each track, with 2 or 3 drum sets and electric bass in the same track. League compares 'folkloric' grooves with the American habit to analyse rhythm with mathematics
source: npr-culcha; liner-culcha; offbeat-qm; bassmag-migration; liner-immigrance; l4lm-film

item: Bo Diddley beat as a cue
content: The drummer and the percussionist play one statement of the Bo Diddley beat to end the Lingus solo. The Bo Diddley beat is a variation of the 3-2 clave.
parameters: 3-2 son clave on a grid of 16 steps: steps 1, 4, 7, 11, 13 (the grid is standard knowledge; it is not in the sources)

content: Sput Searight uses drum sounds from 1969 to 1983: open and high, then damped and deep, then deep and open. A snare with high tuning and the snares off sounds like a timbale. A 15-inch snare sounds like a floor tom or a dark, fat snare. Somni has 4 kits with 4 sounds.
parameters: Searight: kick 20x16, tom 12x8, floor tom 16x16, snare 14x5.5; extra snares 15x8 and 10x5.5. Somni kits: 24-inch kick with low, damped toms; 4-piece kit with a second 18-inch kick; 22-inch kick with 2 snares; shallow kick with snares as toms and a 14x3 piccolo snare

item: Drumming on We Like It Here
content: Larnell Lewis came in 1 day before the recording. He knew 2 or 3 of the songs and learned the others on the flight. A drum magazine notes his 16th notes on one bass drum pedal at the speed of a double pedal. The usual drummer, Sput Searight, says: "I have a fascination and fetish for triplets".
parameters: 9 songs learned in 1 afternoon of rehearsal. 1 drummer and 1 percussionist on most tracks

content: The drummers put soft ghost notes on the snare between the backbeats and play the hi-hat in 16th notes with accents. Fills at the end of a phrase use 32nd notes and sextuplets in the gospel 'chops' style.
parameters: Backbeat on beats 2 and 4, or on beat 3 in half-time feel. Ghost notes about 20 dB softer than the backbeat (estimate). Fill length 1 to 2 beats (estimate)

content: He plays programmed jungle and drum and bass beats on acoustic drums in real time.
parameters: A term from computing. He tries to match the "statistical density and accuracy" of a machine. The aim is the illusion of a machine, not a copy

content: Hand and foot techniques that make the machine beats possible.
parameters: Moeller stroke; push-pull accent; valving; heel-toe bass drum; one-handed roll. Left hand plays ghost notes on a jingle snare; two more snares for fills and accents ("Fauxtek", 2012, 4:49)

item: Floor tom as second bass drum; tempo illusion
content: The floor tom is tuned near the bass drum and played with the hands. Polyrhythms make the tempo seem to bend.
parameters: The floor tom copies beats made for two bass drums. The real tempo does not change

item: Drum and bass groove on a kit
content: Two-bar patterns. Constant eighth notes on the hi-hat. Kick and snare change. Many ghost notes.
parameters: Target 160 to 180 BPM; practice from 50 BPM. Hi-hat at the target: 5.3 to 6.0 notes per second (computed)

content: The most used break of jungle and drum and bass.
parameters: 4 bars in 7 seconds (137 BPM, computed; a linked tutorial gives about 136). Bars 1 and 2 are the same. Bar 3 has a delayed snare. Bar 4 has an empty first beat, then syncopation and an early crash. Producers change the pitch and speed and re-order the parts

item: Break change, half-time, house and footwork patterns
content: Rules of the source styles.
parameters: Drum and bass: change between two breaks after each bar; half-time beat at the same tempo. House: kick on beats 1-2-3-4, clap on 2 and 4, hi-hat off the beat. Footwork: kicks skip beats; full-time and half-time sections alternate

item: JD Beck: half-time feel on a fast pulse
content: A "highly embellished half time feel".
parameters: Pulse about 176 BPM. Right hand: running eighth notes (5.9 per second). Left hand: 16th-note texture between them (11.7 per second together). Many paradiddle inversions. Busy bass drum with a fixed pattern

content: Odd metres under an easy surface.
parameters: SMiLE: 4/4, 7/4 and "5/5" (as printed). TAKE A CHANCE: 7/4. TWO SHRiMPS: 9/4. Extra beats in bridges. Live vamps: 18 beats (3 bars of 6/4), then 8 bars of 4/4, then 3/4 at the same tempo

content: Any tempo fits on any other tempo. They meet at one beat.
parameters: His example: a hip-hop beat at 92 BPM with a shuffle at 130 BPM on top (ratio 1.41)

content: Single strokes and ghost notes with a clear pulse. Phrases go over the bar line.
parameters: Practice: flam taps, paradiddles, singles, doubles. Backbeat on 2 and 4 in most of his videos. Groupings and wide dynamics from gospel drumming, at fast tempos

content: One hand plays straight 16th notes through a full fast song.
parameters: Practice: a fast song of 3 to 4 minutes with no tension. At 138 BPM this is 9.2 notes per second (computed). Also groups of 5 or 6 notes with one hand; the stick bounces and the fingers keep time

content: Open-handed playing with ghost notes in the manner of the James Brown drummers.
parameters: Models: "Funky Drummer" and the four-on-the-floor funk beat of "Talking Loud and Saying Nothing". The band enters at 0:34 with the main pattern

content: Each backbeat and each ghost note has the same level. For fast funk the time is as tight as a metronome.
parameters: He practises time, not beats. About 4 hours of drums each day

content: Four tools: Dynamics, Rate, Orchestration, Phrasing.
parameters: "The Loop": a one-bar pattern that mixes divisions in two and in three. Orchestration: 7 combinations of instruments on a small kit. Phrasing: a paradiddle moved across triplets. Book of 88 pages
where: Exploring Your Creativity on the Drumset (2016)

content: The drummer implies a loop but plays it live. A played loop is not the same each time.
parameters: He copies the "ignorance and relentless character" of the drum machine. Sources: Squarepusher (1996), Aphex Twin (2001), Photek (1998), Plug (1996). He could not copy them and kept the space in between

content: An arpeggiator in random mode at a rate of 1/64.
parameters: At 129 BPM this is 34 notes per second (computed): faster than a player

content: Arithmetic table for the centre tempo of drum and bass.
parameters: Eighths 5.8; 16ths 11.6; quintuplets 14.5; sextuplets 17.4; septuplets 20.3; 32nds 23.2 notes per second (computed; which of these rates the players use is an estimate)

content: The standard bar on a grid of 16 steps.
parameters: Kick on steps 1 and 11. Snare on steps 5 and 13. Hi-hat on the eighths. Ghost snares on some of steps 8, 10, 15, 16 (estimate)

content: "Drunk" hip-hop feel as quintuplet or septuplet swing.
parameters: Straight 50 %; septuplet swing (4+3) 57 %; quintuplet swing (3+2) 60 %; triplet 67 %. No source for these artists was read (estimate)

content: Speeds that expert drummers hold for long passages.
parameters: Two hands in single strokes: 13 to 15 notes per second. One hand: 8 to 10 notes per second. Short bursts: to 20 per second (estimate)

content: A riff of an odd length repeats over a plain 4/4 pulse in the drums. The riff moves out of line with the bar. After 4, 8 or 16 bars the riff is cut or changed, and all parts start again together. The wait for this meeting point makes the tension; harmony and melody do not need to change (said of Hamasyan's use of the same method).
parameters: Cycle = 64, 128 or 256 sixteenth notes (4, 8 or 16 bars). Hagström: 'Everything we do is based around a 4/4 core'. Some riffs come back into line only after 16 bars

content: Two riffs of the song show two ways to close the cycle: cut the last statement, or add one note.
parameters: Opening riff: pattern of 23 sixteenths; 5 full statements (115) + a fragment of 13 = 128 = 8 bars of 4/4; a crash cymbal marks the restart. Second riff: 9 sixteenths x 7 = 63, + 1 added sixteenth = 64 = 4 bars; crash on each beat, snare on beat 3, kick doubles the guitars

content: Riff D shortens its last statement. Riff E puts its extra notes in the middle of the cycle, so the end joins the start with no seam.
parameters: Riff D: 22 sixteenths grouped 3+4+3+3+4+5; two statements + one of 20 (last group 3) = 64 = 4 bars; no note longer than two sixteenths. Riff E: 3+3+2+2 = 10 sixteenths, 6 times = 60, + two eighth notes placed after the fourth statement = 64

item: 'Stengah' riffs A, H and I: 11 and 7
content: Riff A is a motive in 11/8 that moves against the bar and is cut after 8 bars. Riffs H and I are in sevens and make the last statement longer to close the cycle.
parameters: Riff H: 7 sixteenths (3+4) x 9 = 63; the ninth statement becomes 3+5; total 64 = 4 bars; it sounds as eight bars of 7/16 and one bar of 2/4. Riff I: 3 phrases x 6 statements x 7 = 126; the last statement becomes 3+6; total 128 = 8 bars

content: The standard academic example (Pieslak 2007, reported by a later thesis). Guitars and bass play long odd bars; the drums play a slow 4/4 on top.
parameters: Guitars and bass: four bars of 25/16 + one bar of 28/16 = 128 sixteenths = 8 bars of 4/4; played twice = 16 bars in four groups of four. Cymbals: steady quarter notes. Snare: beat 3. Kick: with the guitars. The parts meet again at beat 64. 25/16 alone would need 16 statements to come back into line

item: obZen riffs counted in quarter and eighth notes
content: Long riffs loop in a segment of 8 or 16 bars and are cut at its edge. A 'rotated' riff starts in the middle of its pattern.
parameters: 'Lethargica': riff of 23 quarter notes (5+6+6+6); 2 statements + 18 beats = 64 beats = 16 bars. 'Pravus': riff of 9 eighth notes with 15 attacks in an 8-bar segment; later a riff of 7 quarter notes (3+4) in 16 bars split 8+8, four full statements in each half

item: 'Pineal Gland Optics': pitch cycle against rhythm cycle
content: The rhythm pattern and the pitch pattern have different lengths, so each repeat joins new pitches to the rhythm.
parameters: Rhythm: 14 attacks in 12 eighth notes (6 quarter notes). Pitches: 8 notes. The two come into line after 56 attacks, at bars 7 and 13 of a 16-bar segment. The 8-bar verse has no fixed pattern: groups of 21+19+21+11+21+19+16 sixteenths = 128. Tempo quarter = 95

content: The 4/4 layer can move from one instrument to another, or drop away for a time.
parameters: 'Bleed': cymbals mark quarter notes for the first 1:25, then eighth notes; the kick plays the guitars' pattern of 3 sixteenths; at 1:40 the cymbals follow a pattern of 22 sixteenths and the voice carries the 4/4. 'Nostrum': durations 4, 2, 2, 3, 2, 3, 3 eighth notes = 19 eighths, plus a short tail to make 8 bars

item: Three ways to close a cycle
content: Named 'obliged re-phasing' in the analysis. The band chooses the way that makes the join least audible.
parameters: (1) Cut the last statement of the pattern. (2) Add a value: at the end of the cycle or at another place. (3) Make the last statement longer. Extra tools: an accent or a long note away from the start of the pattern; more accents than pitches; a changed first note on the repeat

content: The drums hold two layers at once: the hands show the 4/4, the feet play the riff. Fast kick under a slow snare gives speed and slowness at the same time.
parameters: Cymbal or hi-hat on each quarter note. Snare on beat 3 of each bar. Kick doubles each attack of the guitar riff. A crash marks the start of each 4-bar cycle. Named the most common way Haake plays on a riff. Other snare roles: ornament; a 4:3 figure against the pulse ('I' at 5:40). To find the 4/4, follow the cymbals

content: The band keeps a pulse that the listener can feel and puts all other parts in syncopation against it.
parameters: Riff in 19/16 played 4 times, then a turnaround of a dotted eighth and a sixteenth: 4 x 19 + 4 = 80 sixteenths = 5 bars of 4/4 (sum computed). Studio click: an eighth-note pulse with some accents; claps cue the parts

content: Abasi likes cells of five notes. They come from the hands: a tapping or thumping motion of five notes repeated in sixteenths or as quintuplets.
parameters: 'CAFO' tapping riff: fretting-hand groups of five notes with a tapped octave between. Thumping cell: 2 fretting-hand taps + thumb down + thumb up + finger pluck = 5. 'Gestaltzerfall': the fives became quintuplets 'in three'. The drummer also proposed accents over bars of 4/4 with one bar of 2/4 between them. Exercises: groups of five or three sixteenths that start off the beat

content: The drummer plays the kick with single strokes on two bass drums for power and adds short double strokes as detail. Blast beats are rare.
parameters: Fill-in figure 'one-e' (two sixteenths) on the kick. Blast beat sections on Parrhesia. Three songs have one short figure at extreme speed. The record has drum samples, but no samples replace the cymbals

content: A piano version of the Meshuggah method. A line of fives and threes repeats against a rock backbeat.
parameters: Line of 35 sixteenths = 5+5+5+5+3+3+3+3+3 (four bars of 5/16, five bars of 3/16). 7 statements (245) + one bar of 11/16 = 256 sixteenths = 16 bars of 4/4; then the section repeats. Drums: cymbal on each beat, snare on beat 3. Kick, bass and piano left hand play the first note of each group; the right hand plays all sixteenths

content: An additive pattern that has the length of two bars of 4/4. Later the pattern is made shorter and set against a slower backbeat.
parameters: 5+5+3+5+5+4+5 = 32 sixteenths (piano, bass, kick) over a 4/4 backbeat (cymbals, snare). Later: 3+3+2+3+3+2.5+3.5 = 20 sixteenths over a slower 2/4 backbeat; both layers play twice before they meet

content: One melody appears with groups of five and then with groups of four.
parameters: 'The Grid': 5+5+7+5+5+5 = 32 sixteenths. 'Out of the Grid': the same melody as 4+4+5+4+4+4 = 25 sixteenths over an ostinato in 5/16 (six melody bars = five ostinato bars); later over a 4/4 backbeat, until a step to a faster tempo breaks the cycle
where: The Grid; Out of the Grid (Mockroot)

content: Groups of five sixteenths with one longer group or a rest that completes the 4/4 cycle.
parameters: Intro: 5+5+5+5+5+7 = 32 sixteenths = 2 bars of 4/4; snare on beat 1. Section A: 6 groups of 5, four times = 120, + a rest of 8 = 128 = 8 bars; cymbals in half notes, snare on beat 3. Kick, bass and left hand mark the first note of each group

content: A motive in 13 against a slow rock beat. The second half keeps the motive and doubles the feel.
parameters: 13/8 = 3+3+3+2+2. Four bars of 13/8 (52 eighths) against five bars of 4/4 and one bar of 6/4. Cymbals in half notes, snare on beat 3, kick on the first eighth of each group. In section B the hi-hat plays sixteenths (normal time at quarter = 140)

item: Lines against a backbeat of another length
content: A melodic phrase and a drum pattern of different lengths run together until they meet, or until one part is cut.
parameters: 'A Crane Came From Van': 6+6+7 = 19 sixteenths against a 16-sixteenth backbeat; each statement starts 3 sixteenths later; after 4 statements the drums drop one beat. 'Song for Melan and Rafik': seven bars of 5/8 + one of 7/8 = 42 eighths; 2 phrases = 7 bars of a 12/8 backbeat; then a 4/8 pattern five times and a 3/8 pattern five times
where: A Crane Came From Van; Song for Melan and Rafik

content: The same ostinato can be heard in several metres. The high notes and the low notes group it in two ways.
parameters: Ostinato cycle of 40 eighth notes = 8 bars of 5/8. High notes: 6+7+5+4+6+7+5. Low notes: 6+6+6+4+6+6+6. The drums follow the melody but keep a quarter-note pulse; groups of four and eight bars

content: Two or three metres run at the same time in one instrument or between piano and drums.
parameters: 'Etude No. 1': layers in 5/8 (2+3), 7/8 (3+4) and 3/8; the first two meet every 7 bars of 5/8; all three share a downbeat only once; layers are cut to keep 8-bar groups; 112 of 168 bars have cycles. 'Drip': a layer at the ratio 8:5 implies 5/4 against 4/4. 'Kars 1': written in 5/8 all through, but the cymbal marks make the riff passages sound in 4/4

item: Size and sources of the cycle practice
content: Cycles are a regular device from the third album on. He names folk music, metal and Indian classical music as the sources of his rhythm.
parameters: 13 albums 2006 to 2020, 137 tracks, at least 39 cycle passages. Sources named: Armenian folk music, Tool, Meshuggah, Indian classical music. Practice routine: fives over elevens over a regular four-beat groove

content: South Indian spoken rhythm. Each group length has a fixed syllable set, so a long odd pattern can be spoken as a chain of sets. No source read here says that these artists use it; Hamasyan names Indian classical music, and John McLaughlin uses konnakol to compose.
parameters: 2 Tha Ka. 3 Tha Ki Ta. 4 Tha Ka Dhi Mi. 5 Tha Dhi Gi Na Thom. 6 Tha Ka Dhi Mi Tha Ka. 7 Tha Ka Di Mi Tha Ki Ta. 8 Tha Ka Dhi Mi Tha Ka Jho Nu. 9 Tha Ka Dhi Mi Ta Dhi Gi Na Thom

content: The feel depends on the rate of the kick-snare alternation, not on the tempo number.
parameters: Normal time: kick on beats 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4. Half time: snare on beat 3. Double time: snare on the 'and' of each beat. Quarter time: kick and snare alternate bar by bar. Quadruple time: the traditional blast beat. Octuple time at 80 equals quadruple time at 160

content: A low, palm-muted, syncopated riff in half time. Guitar, bass and often the kick drum play the uneven rhythm in unison, while a cymbal keeps a steady pulse.
parameters: Snare on beat 3. Crash or China cymbal in steady quarter notes. Kick doubles the guitar rhythm. In syncopated riffs of other types the guitar takes its rhythm from kick and snare; in a breakdown the guitar rhythm is the base

content: Collected for a piece in 7. Most examples split seven as 3+4.
parameters: 7/16 as 3+4, nine statements in 4 bars of 4/4 ('Stengah'). 7 quarter notes as 3+4 ('Pravus'). 7/8 as 3+4 against 5/8 as 2+3 ('Etude No. 1'). One bar of 7/8 after seven bars of 5/8 ('Song for Melan and Rafik'). Konnakol: 4+3. Thumping exercises in groups of seven

content: A change of metre with one note value kept constant. In Hamasyan a cycle can also end with a step to a faster or slower tempo.
parameters: Eighth note constant: 5/8 with the bar at 90 a minute (450 eighths a minute) goes to 2/2 with the half note at 112.5 (example from a jazz quartet piece written with Meshuggah's methods). 'Out of the Grid': a step to a faster tempo breaks a cycle. 'Vardavar': the last section drops to a slower tempo for a new cycle

content: Standard drum practice of the fusion side of the style, not confirmed in a source read here. Soft snare notes fill the sixteenths between the accents. Fills are 'linear': no two limbs play at the same time.
parameters: Estimate: ghost notes at about one quarter of the loudness of the backbeat; linear fills in groups of 3, 5 or 7 sixteenths, 2 to 4 beats long, ending on a crash at the next downbeat

content: A bar of 4/4 and a bar of 7/8. It comes from a syncopated 4/4 bass line with each second phrase made half a beat shorter.
parameters: 15/8 = 8 + 7 eighth notes. The riff runs for the full 13:10. Two drummers. Order of entries: bass clarinet, bass, congas and drums

item: Odd metres of the Mwandishi band
content: Funk grooves and ostinatos in long odd bars.
parameters: Hidden Shadows: groove in 19/4, A minor, cowbell. Quasar: ostinato in 7/4 on D-flat. Sleeping Giant: drum fanfare in 6/8 at the start

content: A line of 12 notes in 2 bars. Chromatic steps lead up to the root of each chord.
parameters: Roots B-flat and E-flat on beat 1 of each bar. The arpeggio notes of the line fall every 3 sixteenth notes (tresillo). Chromatic walk-up notes come before them; approach notes A and D are outside the mode. Vamp: B-flat m7 and E-flat 7

content: The bass line alone is in straight sixteenth notes. From the entry of the drums, bass and drums swing the sixteenth notes by amounts that change.
parameters: Drums enter at bar 5. The analyst tests a constant swing of 66% for the sixteenth notes. Hi-hat late; some snare notes early. The tempo goes up slowly during the track

content: Bars of 5, 4, and 3 beats end the theme. The drummer does not mark the start of the form.
parameters: Vamp 16 bars; A 13 bars (last three bars: 5/4, 4/4, 3/4); vamp 4 bars; solo on A and 2 vamp bars, 15 times; vamp 8 bars; last solo over 34 vamp bars. Backbeat moved or left out; fills in sixteenth-note triplets; one take

content: A funk form with mixed bar lengths in one section.
parameters: Vamp 8 bars; A 24; A1 9; B 17 bars that alternate 6/4 and 4/4, with the last bar in 2/4; C 16; D open solo until a cue; then from A again with no C; fade. The hi-hat opens on upbeats in some sections and on downbeats in others

content: The drums play the theme in unison with the band. Then the feel changes to a fast samba-like groove for the solos.
parameters: "faux-samba" (Pierard). The percussion fills the gaps that the drums leave. 10:15. Database tempo: 146 BPM

content: One bar of 18 eighth notes. Each instrument groups it in a different way.
A riff of 19 eighth notes. The drums count it in a different way from the bass.
parameters: 19/8 (also listed as 19/16). Riff and bass: 3/4 + 3/4 + 7/8. Drums: a half-time 4/4 funk beat plus 3 (16 + 3). Form of 11 bars; in the theme bar 7 has 18. The soloist follows the drums

Vital Transformation: drum break in 9/8 at the start. The Dance of Maya (solos): 20 as 3+3+3+3+3+3+2, with displaced accents. Dream: 15 as 3+3+3+3+3 or 2+2+2+2+2+2+3. The bass player in 1973: "7's, 9's, 11's, 17's, 19's"
where: The Inner Mounting Flame; Between Nothingness & Eternity

content: The usual count of the main riff.
parameters: 12/8 (or 6/8), with the arpeggio in groups of 5 + 7 notes. Not confirmed in a source during this study

content: A groove in 3/4 with a second layer in 4/4.
parameters: Snare on each beat; bass drum on the "and" before beat 1 and on beat 1; clay drums play 4/4 over the 3/4 (3 against 4); 13:01. Zawinul: "a hip-hop in 3"

item: One drum pattern for a full piece
content: The drums keep one pattern. The other parts change.
parameters: Hi-hat in eighth notes; snare rim on each quarter note; bass-drum figure of 2 bars; tambourine. On stage from 1978: a shuffle beat

content: Two drummers play different feels, together or one after the other.
parameters: Mysterious Traveller: swing beat against straight rock and funk beat, recorded apart and then combined. Black Market: straight eighth notes, then swing after a hard tape edit to the second drummer. Herandnu: 11/4

content: Two to four rhythm layers go at the same time. The band can also play with no steady beat.
parameters: Sun Ra: 2, 3, or 4 rhythm layers at once. Piece of 1968: lightning drum, log drum, and more percussion in asymmetric cross-rhythms. A free-tempo groove that enters and exits on cue

content: Straight time: all subdivisions are even. Swing time: the two halves of each beat are uneven. Dilla time: straight layers and swung layers sound together, and some parts are before or after the grid. It is not a midpoint between straight and swing.
parameters: "straight and swung at the same time"

content: The hi-hats are exactly on the grid. The snare comes early. The ear hears swing that is not there.
parameters: Charnas saw this when he put the waveform on the grid of an audio workstation
where: Chino XL, Don't Say a Word (beat of about 1998)

item: Swing for each sound, plus shift
content: The SP-1200 has one swing value for all sounds. The MPC lets each sound have its own swing, for example swung hi-hats with a straight kick. The MPC can also shift a part earlier or later. The result is a grid that is out of line in the same way in each loop.
parameters: Dilla got the MPC3000 in 1997 or 1998; the feel is more than "quantise off"

content: The Timing Correct page sets the note value, the swing and the shift.
parameters: Note values: 1/8, 1/8 triplet, 1/16, 1/16 triplet, 1/32, 1/32 triplet, off. Swing: 50 to 75 percent for 1/8 or 1/16 notes; 50 = even; 66 = "a technically perfect swing". Shift: earlier or later in ticks; 1 tick = 1/96 of a quarter note = about 7 ms (6.9 ms at 90 BPM, computed)

content: The designer of the MPC gives these values.
parameters: 50 percent: no swing. 54: loosens straight 16ths and does not sound like swing. 62 at 90 BPM: looser than the exact 66. Useful range: 50 to about 70. Delay of the off 16th at 90 BPM (computed): 54 = 13 ms; 58 = 27 ms; 62 = 40 ms; 66.7 = 56 ms

item: Size and direction of the offsets
content: Writers give the size as tens of milliseconds or less. The same offset repeats in each loop, and the repeat makes it strong. The direction changes from track to track: one account has the kick early, the snare late and the hi-hat on the grid; other accounts have the snare early.
parameters: "a kick hits 30ms early here, a snare drags by 20ms there"; Dilla called his units "baby hairs"

content: Each track has its own map of early and late parts.
parameters: "Get Dis Money": near-straight eighths; backbeat claps a little early; some hi-hats late; no kick on the downbeat. "Say It": on-beat hi-hats straight; off-beat hi-hats and kicks late, but less than a triplet; snares mostly early. "U-Love": hi-hats and snares late; kicks on the grid except the delayed 16ths. "Fall in Love": synth and hi-hat swung and shifted; kick and snare straight

item: Swing as tuplets and as percent
content: Divide the beat into an odd number of parts. Put the off-beat on a late part.
parameters: Triplet 2:1 = 66.7 percent; quintuplet 3:2 = 60; septuplet 4:3 = 57.1; nonuplet 5:4 = 55.6; ratio 5:3 = 62.5 (off-beat one 32nd note late; near the golden ratio at 61.8). Example of 5:3: Kendrick Lamar, "How Much a Dollar Cost"

item: Recipes with two subdivisions at once
content: The parts agree on the beat and rub against each other inside the beat (flams).
parameters: (a) Hi-hat in septuplet swing and kick one 32nd note after the straight eighth; triplet melody above. (b) Straight kick, hi-hat between straight and septuplet swing, snare and hi-hat a little early on the backbeat (Dilla, "Kamaal"). (c) Kick stutters on 32nd notes or on septuplets. (d) Snare a 64th note early on beat 2 (42 ms at 90 BPM, computed). (e) Drift: hi-hat before septuplet swing in bar 1 and after it in bar 4 of a 4-bar loop

content: The drummer plays swing from fives and sevens. The ear hears a relation but cannot name it: a "drunken" feel. Other devices on the 2021 album: metric modulation, 5:3 morphing, triply nested tuplets.
parameters: Quintuplet swing: on-beat 3/5 of the beat, off-beat 2/5 ("Sequence Start"). Septuplet swing: 4/7 and 3/7 (septuplet backbeat in "Dream of Mahjong")

content: In part 2 of the groove, the layers give two possible positions for each beat.
parameters: The two positions are about 50 to 80 ms apart

item: Smallest offset that the ear gets
content: Players can play laid-back, on the beat or pushed when asked.
parameters: "10 to 20 milliseconds may be enough for hearing a difference"; study with 21 guitarists and 21 bassists

item: Swing ratio of classic drum breaks
content: Swing in the sampled breaks is usual but small.
parameters: 30 breaks; median swing ratio 1.2 to 1 (= 54.5 percent, computed). From the abstract of Frane 2017 (Music Perception 34) as shown in a search result; the paper was not opened

content: The position of the off-beat as a percent of the beat. Reverse swing puts the off-beat before the middle.
parameters: 70 percent eighth-note swing (Miles Davis, "Freddie Freeloader", 1959); 58 to 60 percent 16th-note swing (Minnie Riperton, 1975); 60 percent quintuplet swing (Anomalie, "Velours", 2017); reverse swing: 25 (16ths), 33 (triplet), 40 (quintuplet)
where: Examples measured in a DAW by the author of the source

content: He plays drums by hand and does not quantise them. Writers hear irregular drum beats. The wonky style drops the metronome precision of electronic music.
parameters: "Clock Catcher": fast, off-kilter hi-hats. "Getting There": strong accent on beats 1 and 3. Wonky: "slightly out-of-phase beats"

content: Drum solo by Gregory Coleman, sampled in thousands of tracks.
parameters: 4 bars; about 7 seconds; about 136 BPM (137 computed); bars 1 and 2 keep the beat; bar 3 delays one snare; bar 4 has an empty first beat, syncopation and an early crash; recorded in 1969

content: Speed the break up, cut it into slices, and put the slices in a new order. Layer two or three breaks.
parameters: Tempo 165 to 172 BPM; slices of 1/8 note; no cut shorter than 1/16 in the tutorial; keep the main kicks and snares on beats 1, 2 and 4; reverse or re-pitch single slices

content: He is known for odd metres, especially 7/4. He cuts a classical sample again to fit 7/4. The artist name comes from very fast snare rolls that sound like a stick on a grate.
parameters: "Szamár Madár": Elgar cello sample in 7/4 at 174 BPM (machine-detected)

content: A stutter repeats one small piece of audio. Fast repeats become a tone.
parameters: Usual: 16th notes. Faster: 64th notes and more, up to "beyond 2,048th notes". Above about 128th notes the repeats sound like a pitch. Usual pattern: 32nd, then 64th, then 128th

content: Rate in Hz = BPM / 60 x N / 4 for notes of the value 1/N.
parameters: At 174 BPM: 1/16 = 11.6 Hz; 1/32 = 23.2; 1/64 = 46.4; 1/128 = 92.8. At 140 BPM: 9.3; 18.7; 37.3; 74.7. Above about 20 Hz the roll is a buzz with a pitch. Computed values

content: Fast, irregular beats that are hard to dance to. A track that sounded like a drummer playing breakbeats changed how Squarepusher programmed breaks.
parameters: "double-time drum 'n' bass with impossible-to-dance-to rhythms"; first records in 1995

content: Fast syncopated kicks with claps and snares. The track changes between full time and half time.
parameters: 150 to 165 BPM; much sub-bass

content: The snare or clap is on beat 3 of the bar (half time). The kick starts the bar on beat 1 (the tutorial shows this in its pictures only), with extra "lazy" kicks off the beat. The hi-hats are syncopated and shuffled.
parameters: Kit of the example: two kicks (low and high), snare, clap, rimshot, three closed hi-hats, one open hi-hat, ride; rimshots on off-beats; a different velocity on each hit

content: Keep 4/4 and set the grid to divisions of three.
parameters: Example: kicks on beats 1 and 4; one more kick two-thirds of the way from beat 2 to beat 3; rimshots two-thirds of a beat apart; hi-hats in triplets

content: 2-step patterns: the kick skips a beat, and the other percussion is shuffled or in triplets. Burial puts the hits in place by eye in an audio editor, so the rhythm has small hesitations. Future garage has late hi-hats between kick and snare.
parameters: Two kicks in a bar; no sequencer; good drums "look like a nice fishbone" on the screen

content: Minimal, repeated sub-bass lines and percussion in triplets.
parameters: 140 to 150 BPM; bass sounds from square-wave LFOs, wide delays, flanger and chorus

content: The tempi go from 50 BPM to over 300 BPM; the median is 170.5 BPM. The median solo has two choruses and lasts 87 s. About 80% of the solos have a swing feel.
parameters: Median tempo 170.5 BPM; median solo 87 s

content: Measured in this task with a script on the open data file (not a published figure). Notes per second over the whole solo: median 4.38; quartiles 3.54 and 5.31; 90th percentile 6.24; maximum 9.74 (Coltrane, 'Countdown', 338 BPM). The book gives a mean of 4.8 by chorus.
parameters: Whole solo: 3.5 to 5.3 notes/s; fast solos 6 to 7; limit about 10

content: Measured in this task with a script on the open data file (not a published figure). Notes per second inside a phrase: median 5.5; upper quartile 7.4; 90th percentile 9.4. Postbop and fusion: 6.0, 8.2, 9.9. Brecker and Potter: 6.5, 8.7, 10.5.
parameters: Phrase: 5.5 to 6.5 notes/s (median); 9.4 to 10.5 (90th percentile)
where: 11,082 phrases; 5,191 in postbop and fusion; 609 by Brecker and Potter

content: Measured in this task with a script on the open data file (not a published figure). A unit of the type 'line' has a median of 18 notes in 2.5 s: 7.7 notes per second (quartiles 6.0 to 9.2; 90th percentile 10.5; 99th 14.1). Postbop and fusion: 8.2 (90th 11.0; 99th 14.8). Brecker and Potter: 24 notes, 8.7 per second (90th 12.2).
parameters: Line: 12 to 27 notes; 6 to 9 notes/s; virtuoso 8.7 (median) to 12 (90th percentile); ceiling about 15
where: 4,600 line units; annotation by the Jazzomat project

content: Measured in this task with a script on the open data file (not a published figure). Fastest run of 16 notes per solo, in notes per second: median 9.7; 90th percentile 15.5; maximum 21.7. Postbop: median 12.4; 90th percentile 17.3. Very fast values include ornaments and glissandi.
parameters: Burst: 12 to 17 notes/s (postbop); about 20 at the extreme

content: Measured in this task with a script on the open data file (not a published figure). Median notes per second of a solo; median and maximum of the fastest 16-note burst. Brecker: 5.9; 14.3; 17.3. Potter: 5.5; 16.2; 17.8. Coltrane: 5.2; 12.8; 21.7. Liebman: 5.2; 16.7; 20.0. Parker: 4.8; 10.9; 17.3. Metheny: 6.0; 9.7; 11.4.
parameters: Sax virtuoso: 5.5 to 6 notes/s average, bursts 14 to 18; guitar (Metheny): 6 average, bursts 10 to 11
where: Brecker 10 solos; Potter 7; Coltrane 20; Liebman 11; Parker 17; Metheny 4

item: Distribution of the time between notes
content: Measured in this task with a script on the open data file (not a published figure). Time between note onsets inside phrases: median 131 ms. 27.5% are below 100 ms and 51.7% below 134 ms. 5th percentile 60 ms; 1st percentile 41 ms. Postbop: median 120 ms; 32.9% below 100 ms. Median ratio of note length to this time: 0.86.
parameters: Median 120 to 131 ms; 5% below 60 ms; legato factor 0.86

item: Length and speed of fast trumpet lines
content: Lines: median duration 2.16 s (Hubbard) and 2.58 s (Shaw); range 0.7 to 9.2 s. Median 16 and 21 tones; range 6 to 65. Median density 7.21 and 8.90 tones per second; range 3.11 to 16.36.
parameters: Line 2.2 to 2.6 s; 16 to 21 tones; 7.2 to 8.9 tones/s; maximum 16.4
where: Postbop trumpet solos in the Weimar Jazz Database

item: A fast postbop tenor solo in numbers
content: 270 BPM. 799 tones in 127 s: 6.3 tones per second, 5.6 per bar, 21 per phrase. 85.4% of the tones are very short. Syncopated tones: 9.2% (corpus average about 30%). 42% of the phrases start on beat 3. Range 36 semitones.
parameters: 6.3 tones/s at 270 BPM; 21 tones per phrase; range 3 octaves

item: Syncopation and short notes by style
content: About 31% of all tones are syncopated; Goodman 19%, Hubbard 45%. 45% of the times between notes are very short (below 134 ms) and 39% are short (134 to 330 ms). Swing-era solos have 31% very short ones. Postbop has more. The styles differ in rhythm more than in pitch.
parameters: Syncopated tones 0.31 (0.19 to 0.45); very short 0.45; short 0.39

item: Onset density of piano solos in trios
content: A window of four measures holds 26.1 piano onsets on average (SD 8.6). This is about 1.6 onsets per quarter note. A chord counts as one onset. 28.1% of the beats have no piano onset.
parameters: 1.6 onsets per beat; about 5.2 per second at 195 BPM (conversion in this study); 28% of beats empty

content: Twelve pianists played a five-finger melody at 7 to 16 tones per second. All reached 11.7 tones per second. One reached 16.0 tones per second (62 ms between tones). Timing error and timing variability grew with the tempo.
parameters: All: 11.7 notes/s (85 ms); best: 16 notes/s (62 ms)

item: Speed limits of saxophone, guitar and drums
content: Single tonguing on saxophone is usually given as about 10 to 11 notes per second. Slurred runs are faster. Alternate picking of virtuoso guitarists is usually given as 13 to 16 notes per second. Single strokes on drums: about 15 to 20 per second with two hands.
parameters: Sax tongued 10 to 11; guitar picked 13 to 16; drums 15 to 20 notes/s
where: Not confirmed in a source in this task

item: Swing as a percentage and tuplet swings
content: Drum machines give swing as the share of the pair that the first note takes. 50% is straight and 66.7% is triplet swing. Values of 54 to 62% are the usual range for 16th notes. A quintuplet swing is 60% (3:2). A septuplet swing is 57.1% (4:3).
parameters: 50% straight; 54 to 62% usual; 57.1% septuplet; 60% quintuplet; 66.7% triplet
where: Not confirmed in a source in this task (the page with the Roger Linn interview did not load)
